lesson.title: Making Sure Both Sides Speak the Same Format
lesson.summary: The OSI presentation layer is responsible for translating data into a shared representation, covering encoding, compression, and encryption, so that bytes produced by one system's application are meaningful to another system's application.
lesson.body:
Layer 6 of the OSI reference model is the presentation layer, and it exists to solve a problem that has nothing to do with getting bytes from one machine to another and everything to do with what those bytes mean once they arrive. Two computers can have a perfectly reliable transport connection between them and still fail to communicate if one is sending text encoded as EBCDIC and the other expects ASCII, or if one sends a compressed image and the other has no idea how to decompress it. The presentation layer's job is translation: converting between data representations so that the application layer on each end can work with a common format.

Three kinds of translation are usually grouped under this layer. Character and data encoding translation ensures that text, numbers, and structured data are represented consistently, which mattered enormously in the era when mainframes using EBCDIC needed to exchange data with systems using ASCII, and still matters today whenever data is serialized into a format like JSON or XML that both sides must parse identically. Compression reduces the size of data before it is sent, trading computation for bandwidth. Encryption and decryption protect the data's confidentiality and integrity as it crosses a network that cannot be trusted.

The modern internet again does not implement this as a separate layer, which is worth being direct about. TLS, the protocol that encrypts the vast majority of web traffic, performs a function that is conceptually a presentation layer service, since it transforms plaintext application data into an encrypted form before the receiving application can use it, but in practice TLS is implemented as a layer that sits between the transport layer and the application, often described as running just underneath HTTP rather than as OSI layer 6. Similarly, image formats like JPEG and PNG, and serialization formats like JSON, perform encoding functions that OSI would assign to the presentation layer, but they are implemented as libraries the application calls directly, not as a distinct network layer with its own header.

A concrete example ties this together. When a browser requests a product photo from an online store over HTTPS, the file arrives as encrypted TLS records; the transport layer, TCP, has no idea the payload is encrypted or that it is a photo at all, it only sees a reliable stream of bytes. Once TLS decrypts the stream, the application layer receives an HTTP response whose body is a JPEG file, and the browser's image decoding library performs the presentation layer style work of turning compressed JPEG bytes into pixels the screen can display. Each of those transformations, decryption and image decoding, is exactly the kind of representation translation the presentation layer describes, even though no single piece of code in that path is labeled layer 6.

The lesson to take from both the session and presentation layers is the same: OSI names concerns precisely even when real systems distribute those concerns differently. Encryption, compression, and encoding are real, necessary functions, and knowing they belong conceptually to a presentation layer helps explain why, for example, TLS and image codecs exist as distinct pieces of a system rather than being folded silently into either the transport layer below or the raw application logic above.
